77380.subject: 🧬 Your AI documents have DNA now
77380.body:
The Atlas

Автор: GenAI Works


Автор: GenAI Works

    
    
    Прочитайте цю статтю на LinkedIn, щоб приєднатися до обговорення
Прочитати на LinkedIn
https://www.linkedin.com/comm/pulse/your-ai-documents-have-dna-now-genai-works-bsmuc?lipi=urn%3Ali%3Apage%3Aemail_email_series_follow_newsletter_02%3BBa0%2F4URxTLKSAFiZ%2BPdBFA%3D%3D&midToken=AQFTjFOONAfT2w&midSig=21p_zPLwL7lYo1&trk=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_&trkEmail=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_-null-fz96fz~msq8c177~xc-null-null&eid=fz96fz-msq8c177-xc
  
Welcome back! This edition covers an invisible mark inside everything Claude writes, Altman's six-month countdown for your calendar, a safety filter for AI drivers and teammates that live in a group chat. In today's Atlas Newsletter: Can you spot what Claude wrote? Anthropic is embedding invisible watermarks in text, code and files, and the marks survive copy and paste. Who else is in your next meeting? Altman told a room of interns an assistant that watches your screen and records every call is six months out. Would you let an LLM drive? Munich researchers built a filter that runs every AI driving decision through reachability analysis before it touches the controls. What if your coworkers were bots? Grok Bot turns Grok into an iMessage thread of agents, each with its own computer, working around the clock. PS: Want to collaborate with the biggest GTM engine and distribution moat for AI companies? You can feature your tool with us and reach millions. Claude will now sign everything it writes, invisibly Anthropic published a support page laying out plans to embed invisible watermarks in the text, code and files Claude produces.  The move puts the EU AI Act's transparency rules into practice, and Anthropic is applying them across its entire user base rather than just in Europe. Text and code from new Claude models will carry a hidden mark that survives copy and paste outside the platform.  Files get the same C2PA provenance label the industry already uses to tag AI-generated media.  Models shipping after August 2 have the tool built in, and older ones will be retrofitted to add it. Anthropic is also building its own detection tools, with one caveat worth reading closely: a mark means content was "processed by Claude," not necessarily written start to finish by it.  Paste one paragraph into a Claude window for editing and the whole thing may come out labeled. The reaction splits hard, from people calling it responsible to people calling it overreach.  Anthropic isn't alone here.  OpenAI, Google and Meta all signed the Act and will face the same question.  One name missing from the list is xAI. For anyone already uneasy about it, the case for private and open models just got stronger. Your team lives in Cursor and Claude. Your compliance tool doesn't. AI-native teams are shipping faster than ever, but compliance still forces engineers out of their environment

77376.body:
Forbes Edge

Автор: Forbes


Автор: Forbes

    
    
    Прочитайте цю статтю на LinkedIn, щоб приєднатися до обговорення
Прочитати на LinkedIn
https://www.linkedin.com/comm/pulse/smart-way-use-ai-your-job-search-according-experts-forbes-magazine-h4ode?lipi=urn%3Ali%3Apage%3Aemail_email_series_follow_newsletter_02%3BmCFLnQR%2BQ7aHQIZvilfAIQ%3D%3D&midToken=AQFTjFOONAfT2w&midSig=0LqKU0FFablYo1&trk=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_&trkEmail=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_-null-fz96fz~msq5t5k3~vg-null-null&eid=fz96fz-msq5t5k3-vg
  
As artificial intelligence becomes a major part of the hiring process, many job seekers are asking themselves: How much AI is too much AI when applying for jobs? From being advised to use ChatGPT to help with your resume and cover letter, to hearing recruiters say they are tired of reading AI-generated applications, today’s professionals are being inundated with conflicting advice about how the technology may or may not aid their search.  To help clear the air, I spoke with AI experts and hiring managers about the ways in which they would and wouldn’t use AI if they were looking for a job themselves. Here are highlights from what they had to say. How To Use AI: For research: “I would use it to try to get a better understanding of the types of work that happen within the company and how they support people, because part of what you’re looking for are companies that are going to support long-term growth and skills development, which is what people really need,” says Brian Elliott, future of work strategist and CEO of the think tank organization Work Forward.  To improve your resume and cover letter: “AI can be used to tighten up your resume and it can be used to enhance your cover letter, but it still needs to be your own voice, and it still needs to be your own experiences on that resume,” says Margaret Burke, Principal, Talent Acquisition & Development Leader at PwC. To understand how the current market is impacting a company: Burke says that AI can also be helpful in providing job seekers with information about how a company is faring economically, which can give insight into whether the company is even worth applying to.  How Not To Use AI:  To write your resume and cover letter: Clara Shih, Founder and Executive Director of New Work Foundation, says that young workers with little experience in writing resumes and cover letters should steer clear of using AI to completely compose their documents. She says AI should only be used to help write your resume and cover letter if you already have the knowledge to “critique it, evaluate it, reject it, and judge it.” To generate text for a writing sample: Elliott warns that using AI to generate your writing sample and fill out your application entirely can backfire, as more hiring managers are developing an AI-induced hiring paranoia where they worry candidates are using AI to inflate their capabili

Sign up for free here to receive this newsletter in your inbox every Saturday. You’ll also get our weekly newsletter with an exclusive introduction from our editor-in-chief. Earlier this year I found myself briskly walking across Helsinki to a gym where I met a small group of women in their late 60s or 70s. A physiotherapist was taking them through a workout. The walk, the workout and my earlier interview all had something in common. I had just met a Finnish health researcher running an experiment to see whether a combination of lifestyle changes and a common diabetes drug could reduce the risk of dementia. This trial follows groundbreaking research that has shed light on the remarkable drop in the age-adjusted rate of dementia in recent years. Exercise, it turns out, seems to play an important role in keeping our brains healthy. So does getting a shingles vaccine.
